Of possibly Chaldean origin, this king's revolt against the Neo-Assyrian Empire in the 620s BC ended up toppling Assyria entirely and founding the Neo-Babylonian Empire in its place. Who was he?
Nabopolassar: Founder and first king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire.
A Conservative for 14 years before becoming a prominent Eurosceptic, he twice led UKIP and, in 2024, became leader of Reform UK and MP for Clacton — who is it?
Nigel Farage: British politician and broadcaster (born 1964)
A protégé of Tage Erlander, this Swedish prime minister led the Social Democrats from 1969 until he was assassinated in 1986 — who was he?
Olof Palme: Prime Minister of Sweden (1969–76; 1982–86)
Serving as Speaker pro tempore for 22 days after Kevin McCarthy's removal, this North Carolina Republican chaired the House Financial Services Committee from 2023 to 2025 — who is he?
Serving as Vietnam's eighth prime minister from 2021 to 2026, this former lieutenant general once led the Communist Party's organizing commission — who is he?

Phạm Minh Chính: Prime Minister of Vietnam from 2021 to 2026. Phạm Minh Chính (Vietnamese: [faːm˧˨ʔ mïŋ˧˧ t͡ɕïŋ˧˦]; born 10 December 1958) is a Vietnamese politician and former public security lieutenant general.
Built on power concentrated among 'siloviks' from Russia's security services, this system of governance has been likened to Stalinism as a 21st-century watchword — what is it called?
Putinism: Political system in Russia under Vladimir Putin.

Turkish politician who rose from Istanbul mayor to prime minister (2003–2014) and has been president since 2014, co-founding the AKP. His rule has drawn criticism for democratic backsliding. Who is he?
Recep Tayyip Erdoğan: President of Turkey since 2014. Recep Tayyip Erdoğan (born 26 February 1954) is a Turkish politician and statesman who has been the president of Turkey since 2014.
The first person to walk to both the North and South Poles, this explorer later led his son on a 600-mile renewable-energy-only trek to the South Pole in 2017 — who is he?
The second son of Libya's longtime leader, this political figure acted as de facto prime minister and was later acknowledged as his father's heir apparent despite once rejecting the role — who is he?
Saif al-Islam Gaddafi: Libyan political figure (1972–2026)
Twice Austria's chancellor, this politician served as the country's top diplomat from 2013 to 2017 before becoming his party's leader and campaigning to modernize the political system — who is he?
Born Farid Khan, this 16th-century ruler founded an empire after defeating the Mughals and made Delhi his capital, earning the title 'the Just King' — who is he?
Sher Shah Suri: Sultan of Hindustan from 1540 to 1545.
Succeeding his father David as king of ancient Israel, this biblical ruler's wealth and foreign wives allegedly introduced idolatry, sowing the seeds for the kingdom's later split. Who is he?
Solomon: Biblical monarch of ancient Israel. The successor of his father David, he is described as the penultimate ruler of all Twelve Tribes of Israel under a united Israel and Judah.
A physician trained in Hong Kong, he turned revolutionary after the Qing government rejected his 1894 reform petition, and went on to found the Republic of China and the Kuomintang. Who is he?
Sun Yat-sen: Chinese revolutionary and statesman (1866–1925)
Instituted by Diocletian in AD 293, this system split rule of the Roman Empire between two senior 'augusti' and two junior 'caesars' — what was it called?
Tetrarchy: Roman system of power division among four rulers.
The youngest son of Genghis Khan, this Mongol general served as regent of the empire before his brother Ögedei took the throne, and fathered future khans Möngke and Kublai — who was he?
Tolui: Regent of the Mongol Empire from 1227 to 1229.
As India's defence minister, this politician's tenure saw the exposure of the Bofors arms-deal scandal before he went on to serve as prime minister from 1989 to 1990 — who is he?
V. P. Singh: Prime Minister of India from 1989 to 1990. In the Rajiv Gandhi ministry, Singh was given various cabinet posts, including Minister of Finance and Minister of Defence.
Before leading a nation through a full-scale invasion, this law graduate co-founded a comedy company called Kvartal 95 — which president took office in 2019?
Volodymyr Zelenskyy: President of Ukraine since 2019.

A vaudeville-trained humorist born a citizen of the Cherokee Nation and known as 'Oklahoma's Favorite Son,' he made 71 films and wrote over 4,000 newspaper columns before dying in a 1935 plane crash — who was he?
Will Rogers: American humorist and entertainer (1879–1935)
This Pakistani general became the country's third president under martial law in 1969, and his tenure oversaw the war that led to Bangladesh's independence — who was he?
Yahya Khan: President of Pakistan from 1969 to 1971.
Serving first as Albania's youngest-ever prime minister at 27, then president, then finally crowning himself monarch in 1928, this statesman ruled the country until 1939 — who was he?
Zog I: Leader of Albania from 1922 to 1939.
Who among these was born first?
Soichiro Honda (born 1906) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these four was born earliest?

Stephen Gray (scientist) (born 1666) is the earliest of the four. Stephen Gray (December 1666 – February 1736) was an English dyer and astronomer who was the first to systematically experiment with electrical conduction.
SQL (founded 1974) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four came first?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these is a physicist?
Pick the chemist from these four.
Primo Levi is a chemist. Primo Michele Levi (Italian: [ˈpriːmo ˈlɛːvi]; 31 July 1919 – 11 April 1987) was a Jewish Italian chemist, partisan, Holocaust survivor and writer.
What is the atomic number of Copernicium?
Copernicium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Cn and atomic number 112.
What is the atomic number of Thallium?
Thallium is a chemical element; it has symbol Tl and atomic number 81.
In what year was Carlo Acutis born?
Carlo Acutis: Acutis was canonised on 7 September 2025, alongside Pier Giorgio Frassati.
In what year was Yulia Navalnaya born?
Yulia Navalnaya: The widow of Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny, she has been described in media as the "first lady" of the Russian opposition.
In what year was Albert Einstein born?
Albert Einstein (14 March 1879 – 18 April 1955) was a German-born theoretical physicist best known for developing the known theory of relativity.
In what year did Pierre Curie die?
Pierre Curie (15 May 1859 – 19 April 1906) was a French physicist and chemist, and a pioneer in crystallography and magnetism.
In what year did Isaac Newton die?
Isaac Newton: Newton contributed to and refined the scientific method, and his work is considered the most influential in bringing forth modern science.
In what year was Sulfur discovered?
Sulfur (American spelling or sulphur (Commonwealth spelling) is a chemical element; it has symbol S and atomic number 16.
Diazepam: Pfizer. Diazepam, sold under the brand name Valium among others, is a medication of the benzodiazepine family that acts as an anxiolytic.
Boeing 777X: United States. The Boeing 777X is an American long-range, wide-body, twin-engine airliner built by Boeing Commercial Airplanes, undergoing flight testing.
Who is credited with discovering Microscopium?
Microscopium: Nicolas Louis de Lacaille. The name is a Latinised form of the Greek word for microscope.
Who is credited with discovering Toluene?
Toluene: Pierre Joseph Pelletier. Toluene is a colorless, water-insoluble liquid with a sweet smell, and is partially responsible for the aroma of gasoline and paint fumes.
Who is credited with discovering Pethidine?
Pethidine: Otto Eisleb. Pethidine, also known as meperidine and sold under the brand name Demerol among others, is a fully synthetic opioid pain medication of the phenylpiperidine class.
Who is credited with discovering Polonium?
Polonium: Marie Curie. Polonium is a chemical element; it has symbol Po and atomic number 84.
Born out of wedlock on the Caribbean island of Nevis and orphaned young, he became the first U.S. Secretary of the Treasury and founded America's first political party — who was he?
Alexander Hamilton (January 11, 1755 or 1757 - July 12, 1804) was an American military officer, statesman, and Founding Father who served as the first U.S.
This psychological term describes a diverse set of deficits in the ability to feel or anticipate pleasure, and is recognized as a diagnostic feature in the DSM-5 — what's the term?
Anhedonia is a diverse array of deficits in hedonic function, including reduced motivation or ability to experience pleasure.

This type of blood vessel typically carries oxygen-rich blood away from the heart, though the vessels serving the lungs and an unborn baby's placenta carry deoxygenated blood instead — what's it called?
Artery (from Greek (artr)) is a blood vessel in humans and most other animals that takes oxygenated blood away from the heart in the systemic circulation to one or more parts of the body.

This genus of deciduous trees includes 14 species across two subgenera, one found only in East Asia with low, multi-trunked growth, the other spanning Europe, Asia, and eastern North America. What tree genus is this?

Beech (genus Fagus) is a genus of deciduous trees in the family Fagaceae, native to subtropical (accessory forest element) and temperate (as dominant element of mesophytic forests) Eurasia and North America.

Believed to descend from hounds kept at a Belgian abbey and used by police worldwide to track escaped prisoners, this scent hound can discern a person's trail days after they've passed — name this dog breed?
Bloodhound is a large scent hound, originally bred for hunting deer, wild boar, rabbits, and since the Middle Ages, for tracking people.

This opioid medication used to treat addiction and pain can be delivered under the tongue, through the cheek, by injection, patch, or implant — and is often combined with naloxone to deter misuse — what drug is it?
Buprenorphine is an opioid used to treat opioid use disorder, acute pain, and chronic pain.
Which Mediterranean evergreen tree, grown mainly in Spain, produces edible seed pods often ground into a chocolate substitute, with seeds that yield a gum used as a food thickener?
Carob (Ceratonia siliqua) is a flowering evergreen tree or shrub in the Caesalpinioideae subfamily of the legume family, Fabaceae.
The principal sterol of all animals, it concentrates in the brain and spinal cord and is essential to every cell membrane — yet too much in the blood spells trouble. What is it?
Cholesterol is the principal sterol of all animals, distributed in body tissues, especially the brain and spinal cord, and in animal fats and oils.

The most widely distributed corvid, this large all-black bird is found across the Northern Hemisphere and is the heaviest passerine bird, with 11 accepted subspecies showing little variation in appearance. What bird is this?
Common raven (Corvus corax) is a large all-black passerine bird.
The third most-produced American fighter of the Second World War, trailing only the Mustang and the Thunderbolt, this plane first took flight in 1938 — which aircraft?
Curtiss P-40 Warhawk is an American single-engined, single-seat, all-metal fighter-bomber that first flew in 1938.
First discovered in 1877 and named the following year for its unique double-beamed tail bones, this genus of long-necked sauropod dinosaur roamed Late Jurassic North America — what is it?
Diplodocus (or) is an extinct genus of diplodocid sauropod dinosaurs known from the Late Jurassic of North America.
A onetime clerk for Justice Thurgood Marshall, this Harvard Law School dean was tapped for the Supreme Court by President Obama in 2010 — who is she?
Elena Kagan (born April 28, 1960) is an American lawyer who serves as an associate justice of the Supreme Court of the United States.
This U.S. Marine turned professor wrote a 1981 memoir of his WWII combat, later adapted into a Ken Burns documentary and an HBO miniseries where he was played by Joseph Mazzello — who was he?
Eugene Sledge (November 4, 1923 - March 3, 2001) was a United States Marine, university professor, and author.
This infection and inflammation of hair follicles produces white-tipped pimples anywhere on hair-covered skin, and is considered a distinct condition from acne. Name it?
Folliculitis is the infection and inflammation of one or more hair follicles.
This branch of medicine has no set starting age, instead guided by a patient's needs and available caregiving, and helps those managing multiple chronic conditions — what is it?
Geriatrics is a medical specialty focused on addressing the unique health needs of older adults.

This German physicist turned his eye on the mind itself, founding psychophysics and giving his name to a law showing that sensation rises with the logarithm — not the raw intensity — of a stimulus. Whose pioneering work was it?
Gustav Fechner (19 April 1801 - 18 November 1887) was a German physicist, philosopher, and experimental psychologist.
This field studies the methods historians use — their sources, techniques, and theoretical approaches — in turning the past into an academic discipline — what's this field of study called?
Historiography is the study of the methods used by historians in developing history as an academic discipline.

Once diagnosed almost exclusively in women as a physical illness in the 19th century, this term for ungovernable emotional excess later became the focus of research by Freud and Charcot — what is this condition called?
Hysteria is a term used to mean ungovernable emotional excess and can refer to a temporary state of mind or emotion.

This English independent scientist invented the electron capture detector, was first to spot CFCs spread through the atmosphere, and proposed that the Earth behaves as one self-regulating system. Who was he?
James Lovelock (26 July 1919 - 26 July 2022) was an English independent scientist, environmentalist and futurist.
This Indian aerospace engineer served as secretary of the Department of Space and chairman of both ISRO and the Space Commission — who is he?
K. Sivan (born 14 April 1957) is an Indian aerospace engineer who served as the secretary of the Department of Space and chairman of ISRO and Space Commission.
Shaped by constitutions and produced through statutes, regulations or judicial precedent, this body of enforced rules governs behavior and shapes politics and society — what is it?
Law is a set of rules that are created and enforced by governmental or societal institutions to regulate behavior, with its precise definition a matter of longstanding debate.

This American four-engine turboprop military transport aircraft is a comprehensive update of an older Cold War-era design, and remains the only version of its lineage still in production, with 500 delivered to 26 operators. What aircraft is this?
Lockheed Martin C-130J Super Hercules is a medium-size American four-engine turboprop military transport aircraft.
Often found combined with iron in minerals, this hard, brittle, silvery transition metal is added to stainless steel to improve strength and wear resistance. What element is it (symbol Mn)?
Manganese is a chemical element; it has the symbol Mn and atomic number 25.
This scientific field studies Earth's atmosphere and short-term weather phenomena, with a central focus on forecasting — name the discipline?
Meteorology is the scientific study of the Earth's atmosphere and short-term atmospheric phenomena (i.e., weather), with a focus on weather forecasting.
Named for the river near which its type fossil was found by a Dutch chalk quarry in the 18th century, this genus of marine reptile lived until the end of the Cretaceous — what is it?
Mosasaurus ("lizard of the Meuse River") is the type genus (defining example) of the Mosasauridae, an extinct group of aquatic squamate reptiles.

An English aeronautical engineer who wrote novels like On the Beach and A Town Like Alice, he adopted a pen name specifically so his employers at Vickers wouldn't think him 'not a serious person.' Who is he?
Nevil Shute (17 January 1899 - 12 January 1960) was an English novelist and aeronautical engineer who spent his later years in Australia.
In this learning process, voluntary behaviors grow more frequent through reinforcement or fade through punishment and extinction — what is it called?
Operant conditioning is a learning process in which voluntary behaviors are modified by association with the addition (or removal) of reward or aversive stimuli.
Combining medicine with comedy, this physician organizes volunteers to clown around for orphans and patients worldwide through a nonprofit institute he founded in 1989 — who is he?
Patch Adams (born May 28, 1945) is an American physician, comedian, social activist, clown, and author.

Sitting at the intersection of textual criticism, literary criticism, history, and linguistics, this scholarly discipline studies language through oral and written historical sources — what is it called?
Philology (from Ancient Greek (philologa) 'love of word') is the study of language in oral and written historical sources.
This birth defect results in extra fingers or toes, occurs more often in the hands than the feet, and has been linked to more than three dozen genetic mutations — what is it?
Polydactyly (commonly known as sixth finger and extra finger) is a birth defect that results in extra fingers or toes.

This medical specialty diagnoses, treats, and prevents disorders of cognition, perception, mood, emotion, and behavior, typically beginning assessment with a case history and mental status exam — name the field?
Psychiatry is the medical specialty devoted to the diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of deleterious mental conditions.
What dimensionless quantity in fluid dynamics, expressing the ratio of inertial to viscous forces, determines whether a flow will be smooth and laminar or chaotic and turbulent?
Reynolds number (Re) is a dimensionless quantity that helps predict fluid flow patterns in different situations by measuring the ratio between inertial and viscous forces.
A Stanford physicist who also held an English literature degree, in 1983 she became, at 32, the youngest American ever to fly in space. Who is she?
Sally Ride (May 26, 1951-July 23, 2012) was an American astronaut and physicist.
Domesticated well over 3,000 years ago and grown widely in India, Myanmar, and Sudan today, this plant is considered one of the oldest oilseed crops known to humanity — what is it?
Sesame (Sesamum indicum) is a plant in the genus Sesamum, also called benne.
Native to a swath from Ireland to southern China, this aromatic herb is used to flavor food and herbal teas, and its extracted oil serves as both a flavoring and a scent — what is it?

Spearmint (Mentha spicata), also known as garden mint, common mint, lamb mint and mackerel mint, is native to Europe and southern temperate Asia, extending from Ireland in the west to southern China in the east.
The fifth most common element on Earth, this multivalent nonmetal usually turns up in sulfide and sulfate minerals and is a bright yellow crystalline solid — what is it?
Sulfur (American spelling or sulphur (Commonwealth spelling) is a chemical element; it has symbol S and atomic number 16.
Discovered independently by two chemists in 1861 via its distinctive green spectral line, this silvery-white metal takes its name from the Greek word for a green shoot or twig — what element is it?
Thallium is a chemical element; it has symbol Tl and atomic number 81.

This androgenic anabolic steroid, part of the nandrolone group, is marketed in ester forms for veterinary use — commonly given to livestock to boost muscle growth and appetite — what's the steroid called?
Trenbolone is an androgen and anabolic steroid (AAS) of the nandrolone group which itself was never marketed for human use.

This flowering plant genus, the largest in its family with over 680 species, is found mostly across the temperate Northern Hemisphere but also as far-flung as Hawaii and the Andes. What is this plant commonly called?
Viola (plant) is a genus of flowering plants in the family Violaceae.
Common across Europe and also found in Asia, this large carpenter bee bores its nest into dead wood rather than building a hive — which species?
Xylocopa violacea is the common European species of carpenter bee, and one of the largest bees in Europe.
Taken by mouth, smeared as a cream, or injected, this antiviral medication is a frontline treatment for herpes simplex, chickenpox, and shingles. What is it?
Aciclovir: Antiviral medication used against herpes, chickenpox, and shingles.
A broad-spectrum benzimidazole drug, it clears out an alarming roll call of intestinal parasites — pinworm, hookworm, ascariasis, giardiasis and more. Which medication is it?
The heaviest member of its family, this Southeastern U.S. reptile sees males stretch up to 15 feet and tip 1,000 pounds — and it's the larger of just two surviving species in its genus. What is it?
American alligator: Crocodilian native to the Southeastern United States.
First described by a German entomologist in 1818 and known as the 'marsh mosquito,' this genus is the only one that transmits malaria to humans — which genus is it?
Anopheles: Genus of mosquito. The genus Anopheles diverged from other mosquitoes approximately 100 million years ago (mya), and, like other mosquitoes, the eggs, larvae, and pupae are aquatic.
Its guanidino group serves as the biological precursor for nitric oxide production, and this amino acid earned the one-letter code 'R' purely for phonetic reasons — what is it?
Arginine: Amino acid. Arginine is the amino acid with the formula (H2N)(HN)CN(H)(CH2)3CH(NH2)CO2H.
This genus of early African hominins, which lived during the Pliocene and Early Pleistocene, is considered ancestral to the genus that includes modern humans — which genus?
Australopithecus: Genus of hominin ancestral to modern humans. The genera Homo (which includes modern humans), Paranthropus, and Kenyanthropus evolved from some Australopithecus species.
With more than 2,000 species and petals but no sepals, this flowering plant genus originated in Africa and is popular as an ornamental houseplant in cooler climates — which genus?
Begonia: Genus of perennial flowering plants.
Long-tailed and originally from the Indian subcontinent, this whiskered rodent is a major agricultural pest yet is honored as sacred at the Karni Mata Temple in India — which species is it?
Black rat: Species of rodent. It is a generalist omnivore that can live on a wide variety of foods.
Distinguished by a cube-shaped body, this class of stinging cnidarians includes species such as Chironex fleckeri, whose venom is often fatal to humans — what is it?
Box jellyfish: Class of cnidarians distinguished by their cube-shaped medusae.
Designed in 1959 and partly based on Grace Hopper's FLOW-MATIC, this English-like programming language still runs mainframe banking systems today — what is it?
COBOL: Programming language with English-like syntax.
This involuntary, striated tissue forms the thick middle layer of the heart wall, with individual cells joined by structures called intercalated discs — what is it?
Cardiac muscle: Muscular tissue of heart in vertebrates.

Making up the brain's outer layer of neural tissue, this six-layered structure handles attention, memory, language, and consciousness, and is folded to fit more surface area inside the skull — what is it called?
Cerebral cortex: Outer layer of the cerebrum of the mammalian brain.

An essential nutrient your liver can only partly produce on its own, this compound builds phospholipids in cell membranes and helps make a neurotransmitter for muscle control, and occurs naturally in eggs, meat, and fish — which nutrient?
Choline: Chemical compound and essential nutrient. Choline is a cation with the chemical formula [(CH3)3NCH2CH2OH]+.
The smallest member of the cockatoo family and native to Australia, this crested pet bird is kept in an estimated 4.8 million US households — what bird is it?
Cockatiel: Species of bird. It is, therefore, now classified as the smallest subfamily of the Cacatuidae (cockatoo family).
Nicknamed the shaggy mane or lawyer's wig, this scaly white mushroom dissolves itself into black ink just hours after being picked — which fungus?
Coprinus comatus: Species of fungus. The young fruit bodies first appear as white cylinders emerging from the ground, then the bell-shaped caps open out.
Sold under trade names like Super Glue and Krazy Glue, this fast-acting adhesive family rapidly polymerizes the moment it contacts water — which chemical group?
Cyanoacrylate: Type of fast-acting adhesive. The cyanoacrylate group in the monomer rapidly polymerizes in the presence of water to form long, strong chains.
With evidence of practice dating back to 7000 BC, this field is considered the very first specialization to branch off from general medicine — what is it?
Dentistry: Branch of medicine. Dentistry, also known as dental medicine and oral medicine, is the branch of medicine focused on the teeth, gums, and mouth.
Nicknamed 'Spad' after a World War I fighter, this piston-engine attack plane flew from 1946 into the 1980s, an anachronism deep into the Jet Age — which aircraft?
Douglas A-1 Skyraider: American single engine attack aircraft.
Element 99 was first discovered in the radioactive debris of the very first hydrogen bomb explosion in 1952 — what synthetic actinide is it?
Einsteinium: Chemical element with atomic number 99 (Es)
Named from the Latin word for hedgehog, this mammal family unites spiny Eurasian and African hedgehogs with their Southeast Asian cousins, the moonrats — which family?
Erinaceidae: Family of mammals. Erinaceidae (from Latin erinaceus, "hedgehog") is a family in the order Eulipotyphla, consisting of the hedgehogs and moonrats.

Nicknamed the 'yaffle' for its loud call, this bird has a bright red crown and a black moustache stripe, and feeds mostly on ants on the ground rather than drumming on trees like its relatives — what is it?

European green woodpecker: Species of bird. It is resident across much of Europe and the western Palearctic but in Spain and Portugal it is replaced by the similar Iberian green woodpecker (Picus sharpei).
Once tapped as a source of natural rubber, though no longer used commercially for that purpose, this houseplant native to South and Southeast Asia is nicknamed the 'rubber tree.' Which species?
Ficus elastica: Species of banyan tree.
Working in Feynman's group on the Manhattan Project before co-detecting an elusive elementary particle with Clyde Cowan, he won the 1995 Nobel for catching the neutrino — who was he?
Called 'a bridge between the natural and social sciences,' this discipline studies Earth's lands, features, inhabitants, and how they all came to be — what is it?
Geography: Study of Earth's spatial information.
This waterfowl family member is smaller than a swan but larger than a duck; its young are called goslings, and a flock on the ground is known as a gaggle — what bird is it?
Goose: Common name for a group of waterfowl.
This Arabic word for a 'report' refers to the Islamic oral tradition of anecdotes preserving the words and deeds of Muhammad, ranking second only to the Quran in authority — what is it?
Hadith: Collections of sayings and teachings of Muhammad.
This inflammation of the liver can cause jaundice and, if it becomes chronic, progress to cirrhosis — most commonly caused by five different viruses labeled A through E. What condition is it?
Hepatitis: Inflammation of the liver. Hepatitis is acute if it resolves within six months, and chronic if it lasts longer than six months.
The most widespread of all primates, this bipedal, nearly hairless species owes its advanced technology, culture, and language to a large, complex brain — what is it?
Human: Species of hominid in the genus Homo.

Extracted from a Central African plant sacred to Gabon's Bwiti tradition, this hallucinogenic alkaloid was once marketed in Europe as a stimulant before being studied for other therapeutic uses — what is it?
Ibogaine: Psychoactive substance found in plants in the family Apocynaceae.

A theoretical physicist who studied under Max Born earned a chemistry degree from Harvard before pivoting to nuclear physics — and later oversaw the first atomic weapons during WWII. Who is this pivotal figure in physics history?
J. Robert Oppenheimer: American theoretical physicist (1904–1967)
In a landmark 1913 Columbia University address, this American psychologist championed behaviorism and later became known for the unsettling 'Little Albert' experiment — who is he?
Nicknamed 'The Professor' on The Chase, this record-breaking contestant won 74 consecutive games on a legendary quiz show in 2004 before eventually becoming its host — who is he?
Ken Jennings: American game show host (born 1974)
This broadly distributed genus of spiders is informally known as the widow spiders, including the black widow and brown widow — what is it called?
Latrodectus: Genus of spiders. Latrodectus is a broadly distributed genus of spiders informally called the widow spiders, with several species that are commonly known as the true widows.
Creator of both a widely used open-source operating system kernel and the version-control system Git, this engineer won the 2012 Millennium Technology Prize — who is he?
Linus Torvalds: Finnish and American software engineer (born 1969)
Described in the New Testament as a physician, this traditional author of two New Testament books is said to have been martyred by hanging from an olive tree — who is he?
Luke the Evangelist: One of the four traditionally ascribed authors of the canonical gospels.
Also known as sapodilla, this evergreen tree native to Mexico and Central America was carried to the Philippines by Spanish colonizers — which species?
Manilkara zapota: Species of tropical evergreen tree.
Isolated in 1958 from cow pineal glands because it could lighten frog skin, this nighttime brain hormone turned out to be the body's regulator of the sleep-wake cycle — what is it?
Melatonin: Hormone released by the pineal gland.
Often striking one side of the head and sometimes preceded by a sensory 'aura,' this neurological disorder brings nausea and sensitivity to light and sound — what is it?
Migraine: Disorder resulting in recurrent moderate–severe headaches.

Nicknamed the Swiss cheese plant for its perforated leaves, this houseplant native to southern Mexico and Central America produces a fruit that's edible once ripe, despite needle-like calcium oxalate crystals elsewhere in the plant — what is its scientific name?
Monstera deliciosa: Species of plant. Monstera deliciosa, the Swiss cheese plant or split-leaf philodendron, is a species of flowering plant.
Nicknamed the 'brain-eating amoeba,' this free-living microorganism lurks in warm freshwater lakes, hot springs, and poorly chlorinated pools — what is it?
A colorless gas with the formula NO, this free radical carries an unpaired electron and can be brewed by lightning in a thunderstorm. What molecule is it?
Nitric oxide: Colorless gas with the formula NO. Nitric oxide (nitrogen oxide, nitrogen mono-oxide, or nitrogen monoxide) is a colorless gas with the formula NO.
A Boston physician, medical reformer, and 'fireside' poet, this polymath delighted readers with his 'Breakfast-Table' series begun in 1858. Who was he?
Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.: American poet, essayist, physician (1809–1894)
With long dense grey fur and rounded ears set oddly low on the sides of its head, this small wild cat — first described in 1776 near Lake Baikal — roams the cold steppes of Central Asia. What is it?
Pallas's cat: Species of small wild cat. Pallas's cat (Otocolobus manul), also called manul, is a small wild cat with long and dense light grey fur, and rounded ears set low on the sides of the head.
Derived from Greek words meaning 'healer of children,' this branch of medicine covers care from infancy through adolescence — what is it?
Pediatrics: Branch of medicine caring for children. Within the Commonwealth, pediatrics covers patients until the age of 18, except in India where the pediatric age is 12.

Nicknamed 'banana spiders' and 'armed spiders' for their aggressive posture, this genus found mainly in northern South America is better known by a name describing its roaming habits — what genus is this?
Home to cereal crops like wheat, rice, and maize as well as bamboo, this is the fifth-largest plant family on Earth — what is it called?
Poaceae: Family of flowering plants commonly known as grasses.
This beta blocker treats high blood pressure and performance anxiety alike, and can even shrink capillary hemangiomas in infants — what drug?
Propranolol: Beta blocker drug. It can be taken orally, rectally, or by intravenous injection.
First identified in the 1950s as a radio source, this extremely luminous galactic nucleus can outshine an entire galaxy like the Milky Way thousands of times over — what is it?
Quasar: Active galactic nucleus (AGN) containing a supermassive black hole.
Native to South and Southeast Asia, this non-venomous constrictor is the world's longest snake and has been spotted swimming far out at sea — what species is it?
Reticulated python: Species of snake. It is the world's longest snake, and the third heaviest after the green anaconda and Burmese python.

Sold under the brand name Crestor, this medication lowers cholesterol by inhibiting an enzyme in the liver called HMG-CoA reductase, and was the twelfth most commonly prescribed drug in the US in 2023. What is it?
Rosuvastatin: Statin medication. It is recommended to be used with dietary changes, exercise, and weight loss.
